title: Why a 4 × 6 Photo Crops Differently at 5 × 7
description: A 4 × 6 photo has a 2:3 aspect ratio, while a 5 × 7 print has a 5:7 ratio.
direct: A 4 × 6 photo has a 2:3 aspect ratio, while a 5 × 7 print has a 5:7 ratio. Enlarging one directly into the other requires cropping or borders. Decide which edges matter before approving the print.
figureAlt: A mountain print and paper guides illustrate checking a print crop.
figureCaption: AI-generated conceptual illustration, not an App screenshot, measured result or real export.
cards.choice.heading: Shape comes before DPI
cards.choice.body: At 300 pixels per inch, a 5 × 7 image needs 1500 × 2100 pixels. Those numbers describe the final grid, not permission to stretch a 1200 × 1800 picture into a different shape. Stretching distorts proportions.
sections.explain.heading: Crop or preserve all edges
sections.explain.body: Filling the entire 5 × 7 area from a 2:3 source removes some content. Keeping the complete source means unused space or borders. Neither option is universally right: a head near an edge favors preserving composition, while a borderless frame may favor a carefully approved crop.
sections.practice.heading: Verify the deliverable
sections.practice.body: Space Sheep Studio develops our iPhone print-preparation app. It supports paper size, DPI, borders and crop confirmation, plus export verification. Basic single-photo DPI edits are free; advanced print-size fitting has three successful free exports before Pro. Resampling can enlarge the grid but cannot create captured detail. For a large print order, inspect the exported file and a proof first; the printer can still apply its own scaling.

steps.step-1.text: In DPI: Photo Print Prep, set a 5 × 7 inch target, choose the intended DPI and decide whether white borders are acceptable.
steps.step-2.text: Review the independent crop. Keep faces and important edges inside the frame, then check pixel sufficiency.
steps.step-3.text: Export and read back actual pixel dimensions, both DPI axes and physical size. Confirm the print service’s fit/fill settings.
